hints: First rewrite the rational integrand so that each term has a standard antiderivative.
Use $x(x+1)=x^2+x=(x^2+4)+(x-4)$, then separate $\dfrac{x-4}{x^2+4}$ into its $x$ and constant numerator parts.
Integrate the $x/(x^2+4)$ term logarithmically and the $1/(x^2+4)$ term using an inverse tangent.
Evaluate at $6$ and $0$, combining the logarithms while keeping the inverse tangent exact.
walkthrough:
Decompose the rational function using algebraic division:
$$\dfrac{x(x + 1)}{x^2 + 4} = \dfrac{x^2 + x}{x^2 + 4} = \dfrac{(x^2 + 4) + (x - 4)}{x^2 + 4} = 1 + \dfrac{x - 4}{x^2 + 4} = 1 + \dfrac{x}{x^2 + 4} - \dfrac{4}{x^2 + 4}$$

Subtract $F(6) - F(0)$ and simplify the logarithms:
$$\int_0^6 \dfrac{x(x + 1)}{x^2 + 4}\,\mathrm{d}x = 6 + \dfrac{1}{2}\ln 40 - 2\tan^{-1}3 - \dfrac{1}{2}\ln 4$$
$$= 6 + \dfrac{1}{2}(\ln 40 - \ln 4) - 2\tan^{-1}3 = 6 + \dfrac{1}{2}\ln 10 - 2\tan^{-1}3$$

ai_rubric.Integrating Rational Functions: Split the fraction as $1+\frac{x-4}{x^2+4}$. integration and derives $p\ln(x^2+4)$ or $q\tan^{-1}(x/2)$ from. The final result is $6+\frac12\ln 10-2\tan^{-1}3$.
